questions.prompt: What is the core observation behind dynamic warp formation?
options: Branches can be removed by the compiler
After divergence, threads from different warps often want the same next instruction and could share one warp
questions.explanation: Partial warps at the same PC can be merged into fuller ones.

questions.prompt: Why must regrouping keep each thread in its home lane?
options: Because a thread's registers live in that lane's register-file bank, and moving them is too expensive
questions.explanation: The register file is banked per lane, so regrouping is lane-aware.

questions.prompt: Two warps both send lanes 0–15 down path A (10 instructions) and lanes 16–31 down path B (10 instructions). With lane-aware regrouping, how many warp instructions are issued in total for both paths?
questions.explanation: Lanes 0–15 each have 2 A-threads, so A needs 2 warps (20); likewise B needs 2 (20). Total 40, the same as PDOM: the constraint blocks any gain.

questions.prompt: Now warp 1 sends lanes 0–15 down A and warp 2 sends lanes 16–31 down A (B is the rest). Path costs are 10 each. Lane-aware regrouping issues how many warp instructions in total?
questions.explanation: Every lane has exactly one A-thread and one B-thread, so A needs 1 warp and B needs 1: 10 + 10 = 20, half of PDOM's 40.

questions.prompt: Which problems did the follow-up, Thread Block Compaction, address?
options: Regrouped warps' memory accesses coalesce worse
Some threads can wait a long time to be regrouped (starvation)
questions.explanation: Mixing threads from all over the SM hurts locality and fairness; compacting within a block limits both.
